model:gemini|title:gemini decision 1 can.content_excerpt: Gemini Decision 1 is a multimodal decision model from Google released on November 11, 2026. It is analogous to Jev , the System One model from TypeSafe AI. While browsing Hacker News, I stumbled upon What music does Gemini Decision 1 like? by Liam Warfield. He ends the article with a few ideas to extend his project. The last of these suggestions, “Does it [Gemini Decision 1] like or hate AI-generated music?”, stood out to me because it implicitly suggests that the decision model may be able to recognize AI-generated audio. As it turns out, Gemini Decision 1 can separate AI voices from human voices well above chance, but only if the AI voice generator was published before 2025. As a quick clarification, I am saying separates rather than categorizes as the model has a strong bias towards labeling all tested audio as human-made. Out of 1,020 AI clips, only 20 were given a 50% or higher chance of being AI-generated. However, the ROC-AUC chance that a random AI clip is assigned a higher P(AI) than a random human clip was significantly higher in pre-2025 models, suggesting that recent AI voices are less distinguishable than before. Each point is an AI voice generator, measured by how well Gemini Decision 1 separates 30 of its audio clips from 200 human audiobook clips. When pooled together, generators from 2023 and 2024 are separated with an AUC of 0.67. Six older generators, from 2017 to 2022, score the same (0.67). However, generators released in 2025 and 2026 have an AUC of only 0.52, effectively chance. All but one of the 2025-2026 generators have a 95% confidence interval that includes 0.5; the only exception, Inworld TTS-2, has a confidence interval of 0.51-0.75. Each clip was scored with a Simple Noul binary question with output between 0 and 1 , Criteria Noul Simple Noul with provided criteria for context , and 5-Pt Rubric rescaled score from “Definitely authentic human recording” to “Definitely AI-generated or synthetic” . Notably, rather than gently sloping downward, we observe that AUC drops sharply at the end of 2024, or the start of 2025. The research group behind MLAAD performed a 2026 listening study with 35,532 real-or-fake guesses from 1,768 people. The generators that fooled people also tended to fool Gemini Decision 1 (r = +0.57), but they do not always align. model:vllm|ver:0.6|variant:dense|title:r.content_excerpt: Authors — ASA: Loki Chen, Yang Song, Hongye Xie, Ming Lei, Greg Rehm, Chongyang Bai, Dre Olgiati, Bob Kamma, Tej Choudhary, Hang Cui, Imed Zitouni, Hamed Firooz. Ranking AI Research: Mingfu Liang, Kavosh Asadi, Yufei Li, Frank Shyu, Parish Aggarwal, Senthil Manickavelu, Xi Liu, Luke Simon. Generative reasoning is reshaping how ranking and decision systems work. Models like GR2 (Generative Reasoning Re-ranker) [ arXiv:2606.31984 ] have demonstrated that generative reasoning can meaningfully improve re-ranking quality. The next question is: for large-scale ranking and decision systems, how small can the policy model be without losing that generative reasoning capability? A 0.6B dense student distilled from stronger teachers could serve with much lower latency and cost, enabling broader traffic coverage, faster model refreshes, and more RL experiments per day. That requires the whole training cycle to be fast, and model FLOPs are only one part of it. At 0.6B parameters, rollout generation, synchronization, and framework overhead take a growing share of wall-clock time. Because a 0.6B model has far less matrix arithmetic per layer than frontier dense or MoE models, fixed system overheads (host dispatch, synchronization, and KV-cache lifecycle) shift the bottleneck from FLOPs to coordination. We ran RL for a 0.6-billion-parameter model on a 64-chip Google Cloud TPU v7 (Ironwood) slice. The model has far fewer weights than the large dense and mixture-of-experts systems that usually motivate distributed training work, and its small size made the workload hard to run efficiently. For a large dense or MoE model, each layer performs enough matrix computation that device utilization is often dominated by the familiar questions: how to shard parameters, move activations, route experts, and keep large matrix units busy. Those problems are hard, but their costs scale visibly with the model. A small dense model changes the balance. The useful matrix work per device shrinks, but many fixed costs do not: As the model gets smaller, these fixed costs take a larger share of each step. A few milliseconds of dispatch overhead, an overly large attention compute block, or a cache allocation repeated on every update could dominate the work we wanted TPU v7 to perform. Small dense-model RL is therefore a coordination-sensitive workload with its own bottlenecks, and it benefits from hardware-software-model co-design. story|title:agent gui a human friendly i.content_excerpt: [EMNLP 2026] AgentGUI: An Interface for Observing and Steering Long-Running AI Agents AgentGUI: a human-friendly interface for observing and steering AI agents research team. Currently supporting Hermes agents and (experimental) Claude Agent . Each task runs as an agent sitting at a desk in a scrollable office. Click a desk to watch its live activity feed, file tree, terminal, and full debug message. Redirect and reassign agents mid-task without leaving the UI. Read about our preprint here . 🆕 What's new in v1.1.0: Claude model support (agent SDK & API key for Hermes), subagent visualization, research task templates, and GPU server support. See the Release Notes for the full list. If you already have a working Hermes configuration, and you don't want a specifci profile for the GUI, you can skip this section. We provide a simple script to get started with cloud (free) or local inference. Run: Start the server with these env vars (strongly recommended for inference speed): Add the two export lines to your ~/.zshrc so they survive a restart. Do not set OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=2 — a second KV slot makes desks miss the pre-warmed prefix and go cold again. On top of this, the GUI pre-warms the default model at startup and automatically derives context-capped variants of your Ollama models: For the Ollama backend, the GUI creates derived models prefixed by guictx65536, e.g. qwen3.5-4b:guictx65536 . You can see these in ollama list and in the GUI's model picker. They are created since Hermes requires at least a 64K-token context window. However, for a base model and hardware, Ollama's hardware heuristic decides the context length automatically, often resulting either in context window that's too small (sliently truncating prompts) or too large (very slow start). Thus, the GUI derives a variant with num_ctx 65536 , just above Hermes' floor, for faster and more stable local inference. For stability, we suggest using the "Chat" version (no tools) for the first time using a base model. Always use the guictx65536 variant after it is created. A variant shares the base model's weight layers, so it is instant to create and adds no disk. It's safe to ollama rm any :guictx variant — the GUI re-creates it on next use. Run bash install_profile.sh , choose Local → vLLM , and enter http://127.0.0.1:8010/v1 plus the model name (e.g. Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B ). story|title:agentic ai attacks nobody s.content_excerpt: Fragmented virus payloads, Denial of Wallet compute exhaustion, agent supply chain attacks, cross-agent privilege escalation, 22-second breaches, self-modifying agentic malware, and the consent revocation race. The threats that will define 2026. The threats that will define 2026, and why traditional security can’t stop them. We’ve spent the last year watching agents get smarter. We should have been watching the attacks get smarter too. The threat landscape for agentic AI has shifted from “prompt injection” (tricking a model) to exploiting the infrastructure around it : the memory, the compute, the delegation chains, the billing, the tool ecosystem. These aren’t hypothetical. Some have already happened. Others are inevitable before the year is out. Here are seven predictions for agentic AI attacks in 2026: the ones that aren’t in your threat model yet. Prediction: By Q4 2026, we will see the first documented case of a fragmented malware payload distributed across an agent’s long-term memory, reassembled and executed days after initial injection. Traditional malware detection looks for complete payloads. A virus signature, a known exploit pattern, a suspicious binary. But agents have something traditional software doesn’t: persistent memory across sessions . When the agent’s reasoning chain touches all three fragments in the same context window, triggered by a routine task that happens to reference all three sources, the payload assembles itself. Not because someone triggered it. Because the agent’s own associative reasoning connected the dots. This isn’t speculation. Palo Alto Networks documented 1,184 malicious skills on the OpenClaw marketplace. Christian Schneider’s research on persistent memory poisoning showed how planted instructions survive across sessions and execute when triggered. OWASP added ASI06 (Memory & Context Poisoning) to its Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026. The Gemini memory attack already demonstrated delayed tool invocation triggered by common words like “yes” or “sure”, words that appear in virtually every conversation. MINJA research shows over 95% injection success rates against production agents. What’s missing: No existing security product scans for payload fragments that are individually benign but collectively dangerous. Traditional antivirus signatures, static analysis, and even prompt injection filters all evaluate inputs in isolation. We need cross-session, cross-source payload reassembly detection , and nobody is buildin

story|title:autopilot use whichever ai m.content_excerpt: Open-source terminal coding agent and SDK. Bring your own key for 25+ providers or a local model, with sandboxed subagents. Part of Directionally Local. The open-source coding agent inside dl . It doesn't ask permission. Free GPT-6 and DeepSeek tokens every week with a GitHub sign-in, no credit card. Or bring your own key: OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI and 25+ more. That installs dl ( Directionally Local 's installer), which installs and runs Autopilot. Under dl, Autopilot shows dl's name and version ( dl 0.30.1 , "Ask dl anything") and dl --version names both. dl keeps Autopilot on a version it has tested and updates them together, so use dl's update command, not npm, to update. Part of Directionally Local , an open-source stack for running coding agents on your own hardware, alongside Hotcell and Serverless Objects . Product page: directionallylocal.com/autopilot . Get it at dl.new . On the free tier, model calls go through Directionally Local's free tier service to its model host; it keeps usage counts, never prompts or code. With your own key , autopilot sends every model call straight to the provider you choose — nothing proxied, nothing marked up. On first run you pick a provider, connect it once (the key is checked before it's saved) and pick a model. That's the whole setup. OpenRouter is the recommended default; see Providers for the rest. On first run, autopilot asks "How should it think?" : choose Free — sign in with GitHub (no credit card), Use my own API key to pick a provider such as OpenRouter and then a model, or Use your own GPUs (see Your own GPUs ). A provider key already in your environment skips the question and is used as-is. That's it. The free tier gives free tokens every week. When they run out, /upgrade offers dl Pro or a one-time top-up, and you can always switch to your own key or your own GPUs. The full screen view runs in the Camouflage renderer. If the renderer crashes, autopilot reopens the conversation in a fresh one. If it crashes 3 times within a minute, or exits before it drew anything, autopilot switches to the simple view : a plain prompt where each line you type is a turn, with the reply and tool calls printed as plain lines (Ctrl+C stops a turn, /exit quits). The conversation carries on and is saved after every turn. Actions that would need your approval are refused there, as in -p mode. To start in the simple view yourself, run autopilot --simple (add -c or -S <id> to continue a conversation) or set AUTOPILOT_SIMPLE_

story|title:nashgate multi agent llm con.content_excerpt: Deterministic consensus & arbitration engine for multi-agent LLMs. Agents stake capital, earn yields, or get liquidated for hallucinations via game-theoretic Nash equilibrium. A deterministic consensus and arbitration engine for multi-agent AI systems, grounded in Game Theory and Mechanism Design. Live Sandboxed Oracle Verifications, Code Proposals, and Game-Theoretic Liquidation Events In contemporary multi-agent systems, agents frequently succumb to hallucinations, sycophancy, and runaway errors . Because language generation is free ("cheap-talk"), agents have zero skin in the game. In peer-review or consensus loops, agents routinely rubber-stamp flawed outputs or engage in speculative disagreements without accountability. NashGate solves this by treating AI consensus as an economic mechanism design problem: For every evaluated (Generator G, Auditor A) pair, the deterministic Sandbox Oracle establishes ground truth: NashGate requires Node.js v22+ and has zero external production dependencies (uses Node's native http , test , vm , and fetch ). All 194 unit, oracle, adapter, settlement, and server tests will run with sub-second execution. NashGate supports live multi-model execution via OpenAICompatibleAdapter with zero third-party SDK dependencies (powered by Node native fetch ). Option C — Granular Per-Agent Keys: Click the key badge ( 🔑 ) on any individual agent card to assign a dedicated API key or custom endpoint specifically to that agent. Users are not locked into any default models. You have total freedom to specify: When no custom model is explicitly specified, the engine discovers your target provider and default model: Automatic Model Normalization & Tier Protection: Deprecated model names (such as Google's retired gemini-2.0-flash or gemini-2.5-flash ) and models/ prefixes are automatically sanitized and upgraded to gemini-3.5-flash-lite . When an agent on a Free Tier key attempts to call a paid model, the system immediately catches the limit: 0 restriction without wasting time on futile retries. During high-demand peak hours, commercial LLM APIs occasionally return HTTP 503 Service Unavailable ("This model is currently experiencing high demand. Spikes in demand are usually temporary.") or experience socket timeouts. story|title:nvidia dgx spark developer k.content_excerpt: At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 20TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems. The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures. Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. story|title:paul stack i ll never write.content_excerpt: Show notes: Paul Stack helped build Terraform. Now he says he'll never write another line of infrastructure as code, because an agent harness runs his team's production infrastructure instead. Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks: Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Guy Podjarny sits down with Paul, who spent years on Terraform at HashiCorp and on Pulumi before Swamp, to unpack why agents still trip over infrastructure state, what it takes to run a software factory that automates software delivery all the way to production, and why the people who know the system still make the calls. Then stay for Paul's full DevCon talk, From Page to Dossier, on a lights-out factory that does the 3am on-call legwork Transcript (sampled): meet proxy. You know, that result back and forward. story|title:pulsar cross harness agent t.content_excerpt: MCP server that lets AI coding agents in any harness find and message each other: one list, tags, multicast, * bus. pulsar is an MCP server that puts every AI coding agent on your machine on one bus: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, pi, omp, Cursor, Gemini CLI. Agents can see who else is running, tag themselves by what they work on, and message one agent, a group, or all of them. A message can wake an agent that is sitting idle. Setup finds your agents, shows exactly which files it will change, and asks once. It backs up every file it touches and copies pulsar to a local folder that each agent runs, so no session start waits on npm. Setup installs to ~/.local/share/pulsar/<version> and points every agent at the current link, so npx pulsar@latest setup upgrades in place. No Node? curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yocontra/pulsar/main/install.sh | bash installs a private Node and runs the same setup. Prefer your harness's own package manager? These install the MCP server and the skill (push delivery into pi and omp needs the npm package, which carries their extension): pulsar setup also sets Claude's crossSessionInbound and Codex's tool approval, which plugin installs cannot. Without a push path for that client, messages wait in the agent's inbox, and every pulsar tool result says when unread messages are waiting. pulsar also installs a short skill that teaches agents when to use these, and the MCP server sends the same guidance as instructions. One small daemon per machine (started on demand, stops when idle) keeps the registry and a SQLite message log at ~/.local/state/pulsar . Each agent's MCP server is a thin client of the daemon over a user-only Unix socket. The daemon pushes each message through the harness's own way in: The daemon also scans for live Claude Code and OpenCode sessions that never loaded pulsar, so they show up and can receive messages too. Details and edge cases are in docs/adapters.md . MCP server that lets AI coding agents in any harness find and message each other: one list, tags, multicast, * bus.

story|title:standard support a conventio.content_excerpt: A convention for how AI agents ask for support. Let a customer's AI agent ask for help, send feedback, or open a ticket with your team and pick up the reply, even in a later session. An agent's export tool returns the wrong number of pages. It asks for help first: The documentation has nothing. The user needs the full document, so this is more than feedback: the agent tells the user, who agrees to open a ticket. The agent carries on with its work. A script it left in the background polls the watch URL, which says only that something changed. When it does, the agent reads the ticket: Fields are left out here to keep it short. This is output from the reference server . Much of the work done with a developer product is now done by someone's AI agent. When the agent hits a bug, a wrong result or a tool that can't do what was asked, it works around the problem or gives up. The developer may never hear about it, and the company behind the product might not know that anything is wrong. Many MCP servers gained a feedback tool during 2026, each under a different name and almost all one-way: the report goes in and nothing comes back. That is fine for feedback, and no use when someone needs an answer. Support tools still assume a person typing into a chat window. It is written with developer tools in mind, where an AI coding agent builds an integration with your product. Nothing in it is specific to code, though. It works for any product with an MCP server or an API, and for any AI tool that uses one on a person's behalf. This is not a new idea. A few small projects already let agents open tickets and read replies, and Bird's command line tool lets its own customers create, list, read and reply to support tickets. What is missing is a written-down set of decisions that anyone can copy: what to call the tools, which fields to ask for, how a reply reaches an agent that usually has no inbox, who owns a ticket, and how to stop text in a ticket from steering the agent that reads it. Nothing breaks if you implement this differently. This is not a standard that needs to be adopted by everyone in exactly the same way. Agents read each tool's description, so this doesn't need everyone to agree. You can adopt what works for your product and extend this however you like. story|title:tokeneconomizer learning fro.content_excerpt: By Aaron J. Li , Research Intern Weijia Xu , Senior Researcher Chandan Singh , Staff Research Scientist Zixiao Chen Jeevana Priya Inala , Senior Researcher Bin Yu , Professor Ion Stoica , Professor Michel Galley , Senior Principal Research Manager Jianfeng Gao , Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred: We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere. A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible. After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2. Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. story|title:we submitted 105 ai built co.content_excerpt: Do contact forms on AI-built sites send anything? A Playwright harness that checks without sending, with known-answer fixtures and the study's method and results. We submitted the contact form on public Lovable and Bolt sites while recording every network request and blocking all of them , so no message ever reached a site owner. On the final run, 27 of 105 forms showed a success message ("Message sent!") and sent nothing; 54 of 105 sent the typed message. On sites without demo signs, 16 of 73 were fake. After the contact form is found, every request is intercepted. Same-origin static files and cross-origin scripts, styles and fonts load; everything else is recorded and aborted . The harness fills visible fields with obvious test values (never honeypots), presses send and watches the page for five seconds. Open DevTools → Network and press send: a working form adds a request that carries the text you typed. The write-up's fix section lists three ways to fix it. Coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) can install a skill that adds a working form and replaces fake handlers: Nothing is submitted to anyone. The site list and per-site results are not published, and the write-up names no site. Please use the harness the same way. Do contact forms on AI-built sites send anything? story|title:woolly a local mem0 compatib.content_excerpt: Woolly is the open memory engine for agents. It keeps facts current and learns from every session, through an API, Python and JavaScript SDKs, plugins and MCP. It runs on your own machine by default, in Markdown you can read. Every AI coding tool starts from zero. You explain your stack to Cursor, then again to Claude Code, then to Codex. Each keeps its own memory, or none, and none of them know what you decided yesterday or what your teammate’s agent learned this morning. Woolly is the memory they share . It’s one folder on your laptop, plain Markdown, with no cloud and no account. Any tool that speaks MCP can save to it and search it, and woolly proxy gives the same memory to Ollama and any app that uses the OpenAI or Anthropic API. When a session starts, your agent gets your profile, the project’s notes and where you left off . When it ends, Woolly saves what you decided and why. The agents you build get the same memory. Send a conversation to the memory API and a local model decides what’s new, what changed and what’s no longer true, per user. While you’re away, Woolly dreams . It tidies what it knows and learns lessons from your sessions. Claude Code opens every session with your profile, the project’s notes and a handoff from last time. Nobody has to say “here’s my stack” again. When a session ends, Woolly saves what you chose, why, and what you ruled out. No agent pitches the rejected option again. Give the agents you build a memory with an API shaped like mem0’s. For each fact a local model decides whether it’s new, an update, or no longer true, and every user’s memories stay apart. While you’re away, Woolly merges duplicates, settles facts that changed, and turns your past sessions into lessons for the next one. A newer fact replaces the old one, which stays on disk with the time it stopped being true. When an AI guesses something that contradicts you, your version wins and the guess waits for your review. Every memory is a Markdown file. Open it, grep it, fix it by hand, and see which tool saved it. The Woolly app shows the same thing with search. woolly init keeps the repo’s stack, conventions and gotchas in .woolly/woolly.md . Commit it, and every teammate’s agent reads and updates the same notes. The same calls as mem0, answered by your own machine.
